title: Singhara Flour Cheela: The Fasting-Friendly Pancake Worth Making Year-Round
excerpt: This crisp, protein-rich water chestnut flour pancake is a staple of Sawan Somwar fasting—and a gluten-free option that deserves a permanent place in the kitchen.
body:
• Singhara (water chestnut) flour cheela is a protein-rich, gluten-free pancake traditionally eaten during Hindu fasting periods like Sawan Somwar and Navratri
  • The recipe requires just five ingredients—singhara flour, green chilies, coriander, black pepper, and rock salt—and takes under 30 minutes to prepare
  • Water chestnut flour is rich in potassium, vitamin B6, and manganese, making it a nutritious alternative to regular wheat flour even outside fasting seasons
  • The dish is part of a broader tradition of vrat-friendly cooking that uses approved ingredients like sendha namak (rock salt), kuttu flour, and sabudana

As the holy month of Sawan continues, millions of Hindus across India and the diaspora observe Monday fasts (Somwar vrat) dedicated to Lord Shiva. Among the most satisfying dishes in the vrat-friendly repertoire is the singhara flour cheela—a crisp, savory pancake made from water chestnut flour that manages to be both ritually appropriate and genuinely delicious.

Unlike many fasting foods that sacrifice flavor for compliance, the singhara cheela delivers a nutty, slightly sweet crunch from the water chestnut flour, balanced by the heat of green chilies and the earthiness of freshly crushed black pepper. It takes under 30 minutes and requires no special equipment beyond a flat non-stick pan.

The Recipe

The batter comes together in minutes. Combine three-quarters of a cup of singhara (water chestnut) flour with one finely chopped green chili, half a tablespoon of chopped coriander leaves, two teaspoons of cumin powder, half a teaspoon of turmeric, two teaspoons of coarsely crushed black pepper, and rock salt (sendha namak) to taste. Mix with enough water to reach a pouring consistency—slightly thicker than dosa batter but thinner than a typical besan cheela.

"Mix with enough water to reach a pouring consistency—slightly thicker than dosa batter but thinner than a typical besan cheela."

Heat a flat non-stick pan and ladle the batter onto it, swirling the pan gently to spread. Do not try to spread it with the back of the ladle—singhara flour batter sticks more easily than wheat-based batters. Add a teaspoon of ghee or oil, sprinkle sesame seeds if desired, and cook each side for about two minutes until golden and crisp.

Why Water Chestnut Flour Works

Singhara flour occupies a unique position among Indian flours. The water chestnut (Trapa natans) is technically not a nut at all but an aquatic plant that grows in marshes and slow-moving water across Asia. The flour milled from its dried corms is naturally gluten-free, rich in potassium, vitamin B6, and manganese, and has a lower glycemic index than regular wheat flour.

Its use during fasting periods stems from its classification as a phalahari ingredient—foods derived from fruits, tubers, and certain approved grains that are permitted during Hindu vrats. The same category includes kuttu (buckwheat) flour, sabudana (tapioca pearls), and samak ke chawal (barnyard millet).

Variations and Serving

Some families blend singhara flour with kuttu flour in equal parts for a heartier version, sometimes called falhari cheela. Others add grated potato or paneer for extra substance. The cheela pairs well with tomato chutney, coconut-peanut chutney, or simply with a dollop of fresh yogurt.

For those outside India who may struggle to find singhara flour at local grocery stores, Indian specialty shops and online retailers like Amazon and iShopIndian typically stock it. The flour keeps well in an airtight container for several months.

Beyond Fasting Season

While singhara flour cheela is most associated with vrat cooking, its nutritional profile makes it a year-round option for anyone looking to diversify their flour choices. Its natural sweetness works particularly well in halwa and sheera preparations, and the flour can be used as a thickener for gravies during and outside fasting periods.
